label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
**One assignment**

Last night Jess texted me, more or less, "it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it," and about half the group chat agreed with her. I wrote three replies and deleted all of them. Fifteen texts back and forth isn't the way to say this, so I'm writing it once, here. It's for all of you, but mostly it's for Jess. I'm not mad, Jess. I get why you said it. I might have said the same thing to you.

**What's going on**

I teach US History II to juniors, two sections. For four years I've run the same project: interview someone in your family or your neighborhood about Boston in 1974 to '76, the busing and desegregation years. Record about ten minutes, then write a two-page reflection on what you heard and what you made of it.

In four years I'd never had a complaint. Last week a parent emailed my principal and copied a school committee member. The email said the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." My principal would like me to quietly drop it. I'm meeting with him and the parent Thursday the 19th at 3:15.

I'm not going to drop it. But I'm also not walking in there to fight her, and I want to explain both halves of that.

**The part where she's right**

I think she has a point about pressure. I've spent a lot of the last week turning it over, and I don't think she's wrong. Asking a sixteen-year-old to sit down with their grandmother and ask what she did or thought in 1974 is asking a lot. Some families don't talk about it, and some have good reasons. A kid who comes home with a recorder and a list of questions can end up in a spot no assignment should put them in. Right now my project assumes everyone has a family member they can and want to interview. That's a flaw, and I'm glad she pointed at it, even if she did it by emailing my boss.

So here's what I'm bringing Thursday. The project stays, but nobody has to interview family. A student can interview a librarian or an archivist, or work from the recorded interviews that past classes have made, with permission from the people in them. Same recording, same reflection, same questions about what happened in this city. No kid has to put their own grandparent on the spot, and no kid has to explain to me why they didn't want to.

I think that's a better assignment than the one I've been giving, and I should have built it years ago.

**Why I won't just drop it**

Jess, this is the part I most wanted you to hear, so I'll give you two stories instead of an argument.

In 2023 a student, I'll call him D., interviewed his grandmother. She drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. Not his mom, not his uncles, nobody. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class, and when it ended nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute. Sixteen-year-olds, silent, and not because I told them to be. They'd just heard a real person describe being on the other side of a window while the city came apart, and they understood it was a person and not a paragraph. I've taught for a long time and I can count on one hand the times a room has gone like that.

Last year a girl found out that her uncle was one of the people throwing rocks at the buses. She was upset, really upset. We talked after class twice. It wasn't a fun conversation and I didn't have a neat way to wrap it up. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. It wasn't a verdict on her uncle. It was somebody working out how to love a person and also know what that person did. That's about as close to the actual job of history as I've ever seen a junior get.

That second story is the one the parent is worried about, and I understand why. A kid was upset. But I was there, and I'd do it the same way again, because the discomfort was the learning. It wasn't a side effect.

**The line I'm drawing**

The kids who are most uncomfortable with this project are often the ones who need it most. That's true, and I also don't get to act on it. I can't force anyone to sit across from a relative and open something up. That's the line, and the alternate option is how I stay on the right side of it. A student can say no to the family interview and still do the work.

What I won't do is pretend the history isn't there. It's the history of the city these kids live in. They walk past the neighborhoods and ride the same transit lines. The textbook gives it one paragraph, and I'm not exaggerating. If I take out the one assignment where they hear it from an actual person, most of them will graduate knowing less about their own city than they could have, and the reason will be that it was awkward. I can't do that quietly. If I'm going to stop teaching it, I'd want to be able to say out loud why, and I can't come up with a reason I'd be comfortable saying.

**The part where you're also right**

Jess, you're not wrong about the risk. I'm tenured, since 2021, so nobody can just fire me over this. But my principal still controls my schedule, and he has a lot to say about who gets AP sections. There are a hundred small ways a job can get worse without anyone ever being fired. You did HR for a while, and you left teaching for a reason, and you know better than most of the group chat how that works. When you say don't torch your job over it, I hear someone who has watched people get quietly squeezed and doesn't want that for me.

And honestly? I'm scared. A little. I'm not being brave about this. I've reread the complaint email more times than I'd like to admit, and I've run through every version of Thursday in my head. I don't feel like someone taking a stand. I feel like someone who got asked a question and found out her answer was no, and is now kind of terrified of what comes after that.

But I looked at what I'd be giving up. It's not one assignment. It's the assignment where a kid finds out something about their own family and has to figure out what to do with it. If I drop that because someone with more power asked me to, then I know what kind of teacher I'll be the next time, and the time after. I'd rather be the one who listened to a fair criticism, changed the project, and kept it.

**What I'm hoping for**

I'm not walking in with a speech. I'm going to listen to her, tell her what I'm changing, and ask what else she'd want to see. If there's a better way to build in the opt-out, or to prepare kids for what they might hear, I want to know. I'd like her to leave feeling heard, because she should be, and because I'd rather have her as someone who helped shape this than someone who beat it.

If it goes badly, it goes badly, and I'll figure out the next thing. But I wanted all of you to know where I landed and why, so you're not guessing from a text thread.

Jess, thank you for saying it straight. I'd rather have the friend who tells me I'm being reckless than the ones who just say go get 'em. You don't have to agree with me. I mostly wanted you to know I'm not doing this on a whim.

I'll text you Thursday after the meeting. Whatever happens, I'm buying the first round next time we're all in the same room.

---

One note before you post: I left out your principal's name and the school's name, since this is a public post about a meeting that hasn't happened yet. If you'd rather name them, easy to add back in. I also kept the students anonymous, which seemed right given the girl's story especially.

reasons: The piece says the original project assumed students needed a family member to interview, although it also allowed neighborhood interviews.
